document.title: Pre-filed Statement of Brian D. George, Senior Lead of U.S. Energy Markets for Google LLC, for the PJM Governance and Stakeholder Reforms Technical Conference
document.group: PJM governance and stakeholder reform vote

pages.text:
UNITED STATES OF AMERICA 
FEDERAL ENERGY REGULATORY COMMISSION  
 
 
PJM Governance and Stakeholder Reforms​ ​
)​
​
        Docket No. AD26-7-000 
 
 
PRE-FILED STATEMENT OF BRIAN D. GEORGE ON BEHALF OF  
GOOGLE LLC 
 
 
 
Chairman Swett and Commissioners Rosner, See, Chang, and LaCerte; 
 
Thank you for convening this Chairman and Commissioner-led Technical Conference in the 
above-captioned proceeding to discuss PJM Interconnection, L.L.C.’s (“PJM”) governance and 
stakeholder processes, with a particular focus on identifying and evaluating concrete, actionable 
reforms to improve PJM’s ability to address operations and market needs in a timely and efficient 
manner.1 My name is Brian George and I serve as Sr. Lead, U.S. Energy Markets at Google, LLC 
(“Google”). My job responsibilities include establishing and executing Google’s energy strategy 
across the RTO and ISO regions, including PJM, and at the Federal Energy Regulatory 
Commission (“FERC”), to ensure access to adequate power supply and infrastructure required to 
serve our data centers in the United States. I welcome this Commission’s proactive leadership on 
governance and stakeholder reforms in PJM, and appreciate the opportunity to submit this 
pre-filed statement and participate in the Technical Conference. 
 
I offer these comments, observations, and recommendations in the interest of improving 
collaboration, fostering innovative thinking, and ultimately producing tangible results that lead to 
a more reliable and efficient grid that can simultaneously accommodate the integration of new 
large loads while also protecting residential consumers from unintended reliability or 
affordability issues. These pre-filed comments address the questions raised by the Commission 
in the Second Supplemental Notice of Commission-Led Technical Conference for Panel 2: PJM 
Stakeholder Process – Design, Transparency, and Decision-Making, and are informed primarily 
by my experience participating in the recent Critical Issue Fast Path (“CIFP”) process on behalf 
of Google and as a member of the Data Center Coalition (“DCC”).  
 
1 See Second Supplemental Notice of Commission-Led Technical Conference, Docket No. AD26-7-000 (July 2, 
2026).  
1

I.​
PJM’s Stakeholder Process is a Robust, Open Forum, But Cannot Succeed Without 
Consistent, Active, and Transparent Leadership From PJM Executive Staff and 
Board of Managers.  
 
The PJM stakeholder process is a public forum, and with limited exceptions, open to 
participation from any individual or organization, including member states. In general, any 
person, including non-members, can participate in meetings, ask questions to PJM staff or other 
stakeholders regarding their respective packages, propose new packages or changes to existing 
packages, lobby other stakeholders, and build coalitions. Over the last year, during the course of 
PJM’s two CIFP stakeholder process to address Large Load Additions (“CIFP-LLA”) and the 
Reliability Backstop Procurement and Connect-and-Manage reforms (“CIFP-RBP/C&M”), 
several members of the PJM Board of Managers (“Board”) were present, providing all 
participants with the opportunity to directly appeal to the members of the Board.  
 
Google is not a PJM member, and we do not have voting rights in the PJM stakeholder process. 
However, Google was deeply engaged in both CIFP processes. We participated in nearly every 
meeting, including in-person, when offered by PJM. In August 2025, at the outset of the 
CIFP-LLA, Google offered detailed public feedback to PJM and the Board, including proposed 
reforms of PJM’s large load forecasting process, PJM’s demand response rules to better align 
with Google’s demand response capabilities, and a Bring Your Own New Generation 
(“BYONG”) proposal to provide large loads a pathway to bilaterally contract to offset new load 
with new generation.2 In September, Google worked with a cross-sector coalition to develop, 
refine, and advance a multi-issue package that contained reforms of PJM’s load forecasting 
process, demand response rules and emergency procedures designed to protect residential 
consumers from blackouts in an emergency, and a proposed reliability backstop auction to 
address PJM’s supply shortfall.3 Google was also proud to help lead, and join, via the DCC, a 
multi-sector package that included four bipartisan governors and two major transmission owners 
in PJM.4  
 
As a result of our efforts, and many others within, and outside of, the traditional stakeholder 
body, PJM and the Board had several strong options to address and manage large load additions. 
While many viewed the outcome of the CIFP-LLA as a failure because all twelve packages 
presented to the Board failed to receive the required sector-weighted approval, most the twelve

packages were not all that dissimilar conceptually, indicating general stakeholder agreement on 
key components and principles.5 In general, packages focused on reforms to load forecasting, 
demand response and emergency procedures, and mechanisms to incentivize large loads to 
BYONG to offset new load or face curtailment risk if PJM’s resource adequacy picture failed to 
improve. All things considered, the CIFP-LLA process worked quite well in identifying core 
issues and proposing conceptual reforms. It is not unreasonable to posit that with a narrowed and 
targeted focus, additional efforts to build consensus, including, critically, from PJM leadership, 
and transparency from the Board regarding their desired outcomes from the stakeholder body, 
and a little more time, consensus could have been achieved. Even if consensus could not have 
been achieved, the Board certainly would have had clear options for potential reforms.  
 
PJM has a tremendous, diverse, and intellectually engaged stakeholder body, comprised of 
subject matter experts, process veterans, and the wonkiest of energy policy wonks, advocating 
for a broad range of perspectives and interests. However, if asked to solve basic arithmetic, such 
as “what is the answer to one plus one?,” the PJM stakeholder body would undoubtedly spend a 
significant amount of time to produce multiple answers. Given the open nature of PJM’s 
stakeholder process, on top of over 1,100 formal PJM members, it can easily become unwieldy 
to manage and balance these naturally conflicting interests; this only becomes more difficult as 
the complexity of the issues facing the stakeholder body increases. Left to their own devices, 
stakeholders cannot and will not achieve consensus, particularly on foundational market and 
operational issues. This is not a criticism of PJM stakeholders, but a reality of a large and diverse 
stakeholder body. At the end of the day, market administration and operation is PJM’s 
responsibility; actions or changes have to be justified by PJM and approved by this Commission. 
Therefore, active, consistent, and transparent engagement and leadership from PJM, including 
the Board, is essential to producing tangible outcomes in the stakeholder process.  
 
Throughout the CIFP-LLA process, however, PJM’s position on the various packages or 
conceptual reforms was not consistently known, nor was there a visible public effort focused on 
stakeholder alignment on key reforms, or direction from PJM on acceptable (or unacceptable) 
pathways forward. As an example, in response to 197 pages of stakeholder feedback on the 
CIFP-LLA scope in August 2025, PJM offered only a high-level 19 page presentation (including 
no acknowledgement or feedback on Google’s BYONG comments or questions).6 Given the 
strict time boundaries of the CIFP process, and the volume of proposals on the table, stakeholder 
meetings felt rushed and disjointed, rather than focused attempts to identify and build consensus. 
The process was simultaneously substantively open-ended and bound by a rigid timeline, so the 
outcome was not unexpected. This outcome could have been avoided by the Board and/or PJM

https://www.pjm.com/-/media/DotCom/committees-groups/cifp-lla/2025/20250915/20250915-item-04---stakeholder

Staff more clearly articulating the problem statement, placing more explicit boundaries on scope, 
and exercising better time management to ensure only those packages most consistent with the 
scope received adequate stakeholder discussion and vetting. These are relatively 
easy-to-implement changes that require more affirmative and vocal stances from PJM leadership 
and the Board, if necessary.  
 
The subsequent CIFP process focused on the RBP and C&M benefitted from more affirmative 
PJM engagement and detailed proposals, yet suffered a lack of transparency into PJM’s 
decision-making process, which resulted in last-minute, often significant changes in PJM’s 
proposals. For example, PJM’s initial RBP proposal included a six-month window for large loads 
to bilaterally contract for new capacity, a position supported by an overwhelming majority of 
stakeholders. As Google articulated extensively, BYONG is the best pathway to ensure the costs 
and risks of new generation required to serve large loads are appropriately borne by the large 
load, and not passed on to residential consumers, consistent with the principles of the Ratepayer 
Protection Pledge that Google and six other leading technology companies signed in March 
2026. Despite overwhelming support for PJM’s position, in May, PJM abruptly shifted to a 
September RBP, forgoing the six-month window essential to allow loads to fully explore the 
BYONG alternative.  
 
As another example, consider PJM’s C&M proposal. Despite significant implementation and 
jurisdictional questions, which were raised early and often in the CIFP process, PJM pressed 
forward on a C&M approach that did not provide sufficient detail or clarity. Basic questions, 
such as the definition of “new load” and how PJM’s proposal would respect existing, executed 
firm service power contracts negotiated years ago, were either avoided, defined but then 
changed, or provided with insufficient details. In response, in late June, PJM opted to move away 
from its C&M proposal in favor of a voluntary, registry-based concept administered largely by 
the states. While the questions and concerns that ultimately supported PJM’s move had been 
raised since January, the late shift in position sparked, for good reason, concern among 
stakeholders, including the states, about implementation roles and responsibilities. It is not clear 
why PJM waited until so late in the process to adopt such a significant change; concerns could 
have been avoided or mitigated had PJM shifted stance on C&M earlier in the process, allowing 
entities appropriate time to respond.  
 
These two examples raise two important points. First, we cannot be simultaneously frustrated 
with a “broken” stakeholder process and also frustrated with the positions developed in that 
process when the process is put to work. If PJM had no intent to adopt stakeholders’ positions, 
particularly on the RBP, it would have been easier and far less time consuming to simply move 
forward with a preferred approach. Second, significant changes to proposals have significant 
commercial ramifications. In the case of C&M, an evolving definition of “new load” created 
continuous uncertainty regarding the amount of capacity new large loads would be expected to 
4

procure to avoid curtailment; changing that date meant constantly recalibrating procurement 
efforts. Stakeholders dedicate a significant amount of time preparing for, and engaging in, PJM 
stakeholder processes, and informing their respective leadership of the nature of the various 
proposals to inform commercial activity (e.g., bilateral contracting for new generation). Sudden 
changes in direction, even if well supported, require time to reevaluate the commercial landscape 
and adapt commercial activity.  
 
PJM’s stakeholder process is unique, and as evidenced above, certainly not free from challenges. 
However, like any task, in order for it to be successful, it must be armed with clear directives and 
a level of confidence that outcomes will be respected, or, in the alternative, the rationale for any 
deviation by PJM should be clearly articulated and conveyed with sufficient time for the market 
to respond accordingly. Finally, while every stakeholder wants their position to win the day, that 
is an unreasonable expectation. The stakeholder process is premised on compromise, and 
outcomes will undoubtedly leave stakeholders with mixed emotions. However, fear of this 
should not stand in the way of decisive action.   
 
II.​
Any Governance Reforms Should Be Clear About the Problems They Are Intended 
to Address, and How the Proposed Reforms Will Resolve Those Problems.  
 
PJM is understandably facing an unprecedented amount of pressure, including from the President 
of the United States and the governors of the PJM states. We are in the midst of a period of rapid 
load growth following decades of stagnation. Extreme weather events are increasing in 
frequency, and in early July, PJM was one emergency procedure away from deploying backup 
generators at data center facilities to preserve reliability while serving a record demand of over 
168,000 MW.7 The problems facing PJM are real, and they are here now.  
 
Given this, it is even more important that any changes to PJM’s governance structure clearly 
articulate how those changes will lead to better outcomes for the PJM region. The PJM 
stakeholder process would, without question, benefit from more consistent engagement from all 
of the PJM states, including the state commissioners, executives, and legislators. Google is proud 
to partner with state officials, including in the first CIFP process where the DCC joined a 
coalition that included the governors of Pennsylvania, Maryland, New Jersey, and Virginia. 
Indeed, nothing within PJM’s current rules prevents states from engaging and influencing the 
process today. However, if changes are contemplated that would give states more authority (e.g., 
Federal Power Act Sec. 205 filing rights or a more formal role in selecting PJM Board 
members), those changes need to be explicit regarding their ability to address and resolve the 
identified problems.

III.​
Conclusion  
 
Google welcomes the Commission’s dialogue on governance and stakeholder process reforms in 
PJM, and we appreciate your leadership in resolving the most pressing challenges facing the 
region, and our nation. We look forward to the robust dialogue during and following this 
technical conference, and welcome the opportunity to collaborate with PJM, the PJM states, and 
all stakeholders as we seek common-sense reforms to meaningfully address and resolve 
challenging problems. Thank you for the opportunity to provide these remarks and my 
perspectives.  
 
Sincerely, 
 
 
Brian D. George 
Sr. Lead, U.S. Energy Markets 
Google LLC 
briangeorge@google.com 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
Dated: July 14, 2026
